name: Ivan Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a backend developer at Routewise, a company of about 300 people that sells route-planning software to delivery firms. My day starts at nine with a standup, then I'm mostly in the code that works out which van goes where and in what order. I have a coding assistant open the whole time, and lately I hand it whole chunks of work, like writing tests or a first pass at an API change, and then I check what it gives back.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzle of it. When a courier in a real city saves twenty minutes because our maths got smarter, that feels good. What wears me out is the on-call week, when a customer's dispatch screen breaks at six in the morning and my phone goes off. I live with my girlfriend Dana, who's a physiotherapist, and she's learned to sleep through my phone buzzing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that's roughly the world I thought we'd be in two years ago. Part of me would be a bit disappointed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful but the hype was overdone, which is what half my team already says over lunch. Online I'd probably post something about how good engineers were always going to matter. I wouldn't be smug about it, though, because I bet on these tools early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved for my job and a little bored. I use AI all day, and if it stops getting better I've basically got a nice head start that stops mattering. My job looks safe in that world, and Routewise keeps growing as long as people keep ordering parcels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and push for the senior title next spring, which comes with roughly ten percent more pay. I'd keep putting about four hundred a month into savings, because we've got around four months of costs put by and I'd like six. Dana and I want to buy a flat, so the deposit is the real goal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit flat, like when a film everyone hyped turns out just fine. I don't lose sleep over that world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your head start stops mattering. Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. I spent evenings learning how to chain these tools together, and a colleague called Marco used to tease me for it. In that world Marco would be right. I'd buy him a coffee and live with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What pressures would you still be carrying in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, mainly. We pay about a third of our joint income on a two-room flat near the station, and it goes up every year. The on-call weeks also get old. If nothing changes, the plan is simply to get promoted and buy something before prices run away from us.

say: I'd say the **tools help** but the hype was overdone, like my team already jokes at lunch.
I'd post that **good engineers** were always going to matter, without being smug about it.
think: Privately, I'd feel **relieved** about my job and slightly bored by how little changed.
My early **head start** with AI tools would mostly stop mattering in that world.
Routewise keeps **growing** as long as people keep ordering parcels, so my job looks safe.
do: Push for the **senior title** next spring, which pays roughly ten percent more.
Keep saving about **400 a month** to grow our four months of savings to six.
Keep building the **flat deposit** with Dana, which is our real goal.
feel: **Calm**, with a flat, slightly let-down feeling, like a hyped film that turned out fine.

Put about 400 a month aside towards a flat deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one feels close. Coding is right there in the list, and we're already halfway into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is the moment to get good at directing AI, not to fight it. Online I'd write threads about how I use agents to ship features, because that's how you get noticed when hiring tightens. I'd be honest that some roles go, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Routewise would stop hiring juniors and maybe let a few mid-level people go, and I'm mid-level. I'm average at the pure coding, but I'm better than most at using the tools, so I think I'd survive the first round. Survive isn't the same as safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Inside three months I'd pitch myself to lead the project that puts an AI assistant into our dispatch product, because that's where the budget will go. I'd lift savings to about six hundred a month and skip the trip to Lisbon we'd planned. I'd also update my CV and keep two or three recruiters warm, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a busy way. I'd be nervous and a bit excited at the same time, which is how I felt starting this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our QA team, the people who test the software before release. There are four of them and a lot of their checking is exactly what these tools do well. One of them, Hannah, has a kid on the way. I'd quietly tell her to learn the test automation tools before someone decides for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd survive the first round. What about the second?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second round is when they look at whether one strong developer plus agents can replace three average ones. I'm honest that I'm average at the raw coding. So my job becomes being the person who knows how our routing system actually behaves with real customers, because the tools still don't know that.

I'd post **threads online** about using agents, because visibility counts when hiring tightens.
think: I expect Routewise to **stop hiring juniors** and possibly cut a few mid-level developers like me.

Raise savings to about **600 a month** and cancel the planned Lisbon trip.
Refresh my **CV** and keep two or three recruiters in touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's next year's planning cycle and the one after. That's basically now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say we need a plan for people, not just for companies, because I'd mean it. At work I'd keep my head down and look useful. I wouldn't post much, honestly, because I don't know what I'd say that isn't panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think my job is gone by 2029. If AI can do any thinking work better and cheaper, then a mid-level backend developer is one of the first things a company stops paying for. My whole edge was being good with the tools, and in that world the tools don't need me to drive them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd save everything I could, maybe a thousand a month, and drop the flat deposit idea to keep cash. I'd look at the robot side, because robots are three years behind, and someone has to install and fix them in warehouses. I'd ask our hardware partner, the firm that fits the van trackers, whether they'd take me on in field work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My chest gets tight just picturing the email from HR. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Dana? How does her work look in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the strange part. I always assumed I had the safer career. My girlfriend Dana's physio work is hands-on, so she gets three extra years before the robots. She'd probably be carrying our rent for a while, and I'd hate that, but we'd manage on one income if we moved somewhere cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes first if you lose the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flat by the station. We'd move further out, maybe to the town where Dana's parents live, where rent is half. The car would go too, since I only use it at weekends. Those two alone save us about eight hundred a month.

At work I'd **keep my head down** and post very little, unsure what isn't panic.

Ask the **van-tracker partner** about field work installing and fixing hardware.
Plan a **move further out** near Dana's parents, where rent is half.

fieldNote: He flips his own assumption: his girlfriend's **hands-on job** now looks safer than his.
He sees the **three-year robot gap** as his escape route into field hardware work.
Moving near **Dana's parents** and selling the car would save about 800 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to do something sensible instead of something scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the window to retrain, and I'd say it loudly to people my age. At work I'd argue Routewise should move people into the robot side of delivery, like loading and depot systems. I'd be the guy forwarding courses to the team chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my desk job still goes by 2031, but five years is enough to land somewhere that lasts a few more years after that. Robots come in 2034, so working on robots in real depots gives me until then and maybe longer, since someone has to set them up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd take an evening course in industrial robotics and electronics, roughly two thousand all in, and ask Routewise to move me onto the depot hardware integration team. I'd keep saving about six hundred a month. Dana and I would still buy a small flat, but a cheaper one further out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. It's the kind of worry that makes me get up and do things rather than lie there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots come in 2034. Doesn't that just push the problem back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it does. But three extra years at my age is a lot. I'd be thirty-five by then, with real skills in hardware and software, and that mix is rarer than plain coding. I'm not pretending it's forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who's a developer and isn't doing anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my friend Omar, who builds websites for a bank, to stop assuming it'll be someone else. I'd send him the course link and offer to do it together on Tuesday nights. He'd probably laugh, but he'd come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and final picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Same ending, but that's a whole career phase. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's not waste it arguing whether it's real. I'd probably write about how developers can move toward hardware, data centres and the physical side. At work I'd say keep shipping, there's plenty to build before 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the next few years look fine for me in this one. My job carries on, AI makes me faster, and I can learn the hardware side without rushing. What bothers me is that ten years is long enough to get lazy, and I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the senior role, buy the flat with Dana as planned, and start one course a year on the hardware side. I'd keep about five hundred a month going into savings and put some into an index fund. Around year five I'd make the actual switch, before the crowd does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's background noise. It's like knowing the lease ends in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might get lazy. What would stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dates. I'd put 2031 in my calendar as the year I must be working on hardware, not just learning about it. Dana is good at holding me to things like that. She once made me sign up for a half marathon so I'd stop talking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the decade change your family plans at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes them possible. We'd marry and maybe have a kid around thirty-one. A decade lets us do things in order instead of all at once. By the time AGI arrives I'd want to be in a job with a body in it.

I'd write about developers moving into **hardware** and data centres, and keep shipping at work.

My real risk is getting **lazy** with ten years of runway, and I know myself.

Take **one hardware course** a year and switch fields around year five.
Save about **500 a month**, with some going into an index fund.
feel: **Uneasy** as background noise, like knowing a lease ends in **ten years**.

fieldNote: With ten years, his own job feels **secure for now**; the worry sits in the background.
He fears his own **complacency** more than the technology and sets 2031 as a hard date.
The decade lets him keep **marriage and a child** on schedule with Dana.

steps.text: Take one hardware or electronics course each year
Go for the senior role and keep shipping at Routewise
Put part of monthly savings into an index fund
Buy the flat and plan marriage with Dana as intended

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because two years isn't enough time to retrain and I'd be doing it scared. What would help is a paid way to move sideways, like employers or the state funding a year of hardware training for desk workers. Even half pay while I learned would change everything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what we tell the people coming after us. My cousin is starting a computer science degree next year, and I genuinely don't know whether to tell him to go. I think I'd tell him to do it, but to spend every summer on something you can touch.

headlineQuote: My cousin is starting a computer science degree next year, and I genuinely don't know whether to tell him to go.
portrait: Ivan is a **27-year-old backend developer** at Routewise, a route-planning software firm, living with his physiotherapist girlfriend Dana.
He uses **AI tools all day** and is candid that he is only average at raw coding.
He is calm in AI Plateau, uneasy in Steady Disruption, and **alarmed** if AGI arrives by 2028.
His escape route is the **robot gap**: moving into hardware and depot robotics work.
With more warning, he plans **in order**: senior role, flat, marriage, then a switch around 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to retrain and he would be doing it scared.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid route sideways**, such as a funded year of hardware training for desk workers.
Even **half pay** while learning would change everything for him.
